claim: An intersectional viral vector approach led to the expression of hM4Di-mCherry and/or Chr2-YFP on average in 248±71 mPFC pyramidal neurons (n=3 rats).
source: This approach led to the expression of hM4Di-mCherry and/or Chr2-YFP on average in 248±71 mPFC pyramidal neurons (n=3 rats) that were located in layer 5/6 (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific quantitative data (248±71 neurons) from experimental measurements in 3 rats.

claim: Transfected neurons expressing hM4Di-mCherry and/or Chr2-YFP were located in layer 5/6 of the mPFC.
source: This approach led to the expression of hM4Di-mCherry and/or Chr2-YFP on average in 248±71 mPFC pyramidal neurons (n=3 rats) that were located in layer 5/6 (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: The manuscript states the anatomical location and references Figure 1B and C showing the distribution.

evidence: The manuscript provides specific quantitative data from experimental measurements.

claim: 23.9±3.3% of labelled neurons expressed hM4Di only.

evidence: The manuscript provides specific quantitative data from experimental measurements.

claim: No cells expressed ChR2-EYFP alone.
source: Colocalisation of hM4Di-mCherry and Chr2-EYFP was found in 76.1±3.3% of labelled neurons with 23.9±3.3% expressing hM4Di only and no cells that expressed ChR2-EYFP alone.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific quantitative data from experimental measurements.

claim: The majority of labelled neurons were found in the PrL cortex (72±1.5%) compared to medial orbital cortex (10.8±4.6%).
source: The majority of labelled neurons were found in the PrL cortex (PrL vs medial orbital 72±1.5% vs 10.8±4.6%; Figure 1D and E).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific quantitative data and references figures showing the distribution.

claim: Successful targeting of the PrL-P neurons was confirmed by the presence of hM4Di-mCherry and Chr2-EYFP labelled fibres within the ventrolateral PAG.
source: Successful targeting of the PrL-P neurons was confirmed by the presence of hM4Di-mCherry and Chr2-EYFP labelled fibres within the ventrolateral (vl)PAG (Figure 1F).
evidence: The manuscript describes anatomical confirmation with reference to Figure 1F.

claim: In control animals without CAV–CMV–CRE delivery to the vlPAG, there was negligible expression of actuator protein in the mPFC after delivery of Cre-dependent AAV vectors.
source: In control animals, in which no CAV–CMV–CRE was delivered to the vlPAG, there was negligible expression of actuator protein in the mPFC after delivery of Cre-dependent AAV vectors (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript describes control experiment results with reference to a figure.

claim: Opto-activation of PrL-P neurons in NaivePrL-P.ChR2-hM4Di rats produced a significant increase in thermal withdrawal latencies ipsilateral to the transfected PrL-P pathway (baseline vs PrL-P opto-activation=7.5±0.4 vs 10.4±0.9 s, p=0.008).
source: Opto-activation of PrL-P neurons (10–15 mW, 20 Hz, 10 ms pulse) in NaivePrL-P.ChR2-hM4Di rats produced a significant increase in thermal withdrawal latencies ipsilateral, but not contralateral, to the transfected PrL-P pathway (baseline vs PrL-P opto-activation=7.5±0.4 vs 10.4±0.9 s, p=0.008, paired t-test, n=10; ; Figure 2B and C).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific quantitative data with statistical analysis from behavioral experiments.

claim: Opto-activation of PrL-P neurons did not alter contralateral thermal withdrawal latencies in NaivePrL-P.ChR2-hM4Di rats.
source: Opto-activation of PrL-P neurons (10–15 mW, 20 Hz, 10 ms pulse) in NaivePrL-P.ChR2-hM4Di rats produced a significant increase in thermal withdrawal latencies ipsilateral, but not contralateral, to the transfected PrL-P pathway (baseline vs PrL-P opto-activation=7.5±0.4 vs 10.4±0.9 s, p=0.008, paired t-test, n=10; ; Figure 2B and C).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific quantitative data with statistical analysis from behavioral experiments.

claim: Equivalent illumination in NaivePrL-P.Control rats did not alter ipsilateral or contralateral withdrawal latencies.
source: The equivalent illumination paradigm in NaivePrL-P.Control rats did not alter ipsilateral or contralateral withdrawal latencies (Figure 2B, C and D).
evidence: The manuscript describes control experiment results with reference to figures.

claim: Chemo-inhibition (2.5 mg·kg−1 CNO i.p.) of PrL-P neurons in NaivePrL-P.ChR2-hM4Di rats significantly decreased the average withdrawal ipsilateral to the transfected PrL-P pathway (Baseline vs chemo-inhibition of PrL-P=10.3±0.6 vs 8.3±0.6s, p=0.006).
source: Conversely, chemo-inhibition (2.5 mg·kg−1 CNO i.p.) of PrL-P neurons in the same NaivePrL-P.ChR2-hM4Di rats that received opto-activation significantly decreased the average withdrawal ipsilateral, but not contralateral, to the transfected PrL-P pathway. (Baseline vs chemo-inhibition of PrL-P=10.3±0.6 vs 8.3±0.6s, p=0.006, paired t-test, n=15; Figure 2E and F.)
evidence: The manuscript provides specific quantitative data with statistical analysis from behavioral experiments.

claim: Chemo-inhibition of PrL-P neurons did not affect contralateral withdrawal in NaivePrL-P.ChR2-hM4Di rats.
source: Conversely, chemo-inhibition (2.5 mg·kg−1 CNO i.p.) of PrL-P neurons in the same NaivePrL-P.ChR2-hM4Di rats that received opto-activation significantly decreased the average withdrawal ipsilateral, but not contralateral, to the transfected PrL-P pathway. (Baseline vs chemo-inhibition of PrL-P=10.3±0.6 vs 8.3±0.6s, p=0.006, paired t-test, n=15; Figure 2E and F.)
evidence: The manuscript provides specific quantitative data with statistical analysis from behavioral experiments.

claim: CNO had no significant effect on withdrawal thresholds in NaivePrL-P.Control rats.
source: CNO had no significant effect on withdrawal thresholds in NaivePrL-P.ChR2-hM4Di rats (Figure 2E and F).
evidence: The manuscript describes control experiment results with reference to figures.

claim: There is a tonic level of activity within the PrL-P pathway that dynamically regulates nociception in the absence of any process of sensitization.
source: These findings demonstrate that there is a tonic level of activity within the PrL-P pathway that dynamically regulates nociception in the absence of any process of sensitization.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results showing bidirectional control of nociception.

claim: Chemo-inhibition of PrL-P neurons unmasked mechanical hypersensitivity in TNTPrL-P.ChR2-hM4Di rats at day 3 post-nerve injury, reducing mechanical withdrawal threshold by 80% on average (from 6.0±1.3 g pre-CNO to 1.2±0.5 g post-CNO, p=0.008).
source: Chemo-inhibition of PrL-P neurons unmasked mechanical and cold hypersensitivity in TNT PrL-P.ChR2-h M4Di rats, for the ipsilateral, nerve-injured, hindpaw at day 3 post-nerve injury (Figure 3E and I). The mechanical withdrawal threshold (von Frey [vF]) was reduced on average by 80% on day 3 post-TNT, from 6.0±1.3 g (pre-CNO) to 1.2±0.5 g (post-CNO) (two-way ANOVA, CNO F(1,30)=20.09, p=0.0001; Sidak's post-test day 3 pre-CNO vs post-CNO, p=0.008, n=16; Figure 3E).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific quantitative data with statistical analysis from behavioral experiments.

claim: The number of cold-evoked nocicifensive behaviours was significantly increased ipsilaterally by PrL-P chemo-inhibition at day 3 post-TNT from 2.8±0.5 to 5.8±0.7 events (p=0.003).
source: Similarly, the number of cold-evoked nocicifensive behaviours (foot flicking, biting, and grooming) was significantly increased ipsilaterally by PrL-P chemo-inhibition at day 3 post-TNT from 2.8±0.5 to 5.8±0.7 events (two-way ANOVA, CNO F(1,30)=9.6, p=0.004; Sidak's post-test day 3 pre-CNO vs post-CNO, p=0.003, n=16; Figure 3I).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific quantitative data with statistical analysis from behavioral experiments.

claim: At 7 days post-nerve injury, PrL-P chemo-inhibition significantly decreased the ipsilateral mechanical withdrawal threshold from 2.5±0.5 to 0.30±0.06 g (p=0.001).
source: At 7 days post-nerve injury, PrL-P chemo-inhibition also significantly decreased the ipsilateral mechanical withdrawal threshold from 2.5±0.5 to 0.30±0.06 g (two-way ANOVA, CNO F(1,30)=20.09, p=0.0001; Sidak's post-test p=0.001, n = 16; Figure 3E).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific quantitative data with statistical analysis from behavioral experiments.

claim: PrL-P chemo-inhibition significantly reduced contralateral mechanical withdrawal thresholds at day 3 post-TNT from 13.5±0.7 to 9.0±1.4 g (p=0.03) but not thereafter.
source: For the contralateral (uninjured) paw, PrL-P chemo-inhibition significantly reduced mechanical withdrawal thresholds at day 3 post-TNT from 13.5±0.7 to 9.0±1.4 g (two-way ANOVA, CNO F(1,30)=5.77, p=0.02; Sidak's post-test day 3 pre-CNO vs post-CNO, p=0.03, n=16) but not thereafter (Figure 3F).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific quantitative data with statistical analysis from behavioral experiments.

claim: From 14 days post-nerve injury and up to 42 days, PrL-P chemo-inhibition ceased to significantly change either mechanical or cold-evoked nocifensive behaviour on the ipsilateral hindpaw.
source: From 14 days post-nerve injury and up to 42 days, PrL-P chemo-inhibition ceased to significantly change either mechanical or cold-evoked nocifensive behaviour on the ipsilateral hindpaw (Figure 3E and I, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific quantitative data with statistical analysis from behavioral experiments.

claim: In TNTPrL-P.Control rats, CNO failed to significantly change either mechanical withdrawal thresholds or cold (acetone)-evoked nocicfensive behaviour on either the ipsilateral or contralateral paw at any timepoint post-TNT.
source: In TNTPrL-P.Control rats, CNO failed to significantly change either mechanical withdrawal thresholds or cold (acetone)-evoked nocicfensive behaviour on either the ipsilateral or contralateral paw at any timepoint post-TNT (Figure 3G,H,I, and K).
evidence: The manuscript describes control experiment results with reference to figures.

claim: An equivalent vehicle injection delivered at 7 days post-nerve injury did not affect pain-like behaviour in TNTPrL-P.ChR2-hM4Di rats.
source: Additonally, an equivalent vehicle injection delivered at 7 days post-nerve injury did not affect pain-like behaviour in TNTPrL-P.ChR2-hM4Di rats (Figure 3—figure supplement 2)
evidence: The manuscript describes control experiment results with reference to a figure.

claim: PrL-P neurons provide a tonic descending drive to oppose peripheral sensitisation during the early stages of the development of neuropathic pain, but this effect is lost as sensitisation becomes established after 14 days.
source: These results suggest that PrL-P neurons provide a tonic descending drive to oppose peripheral sensitisation during the early stages of the development of neuropathic pain, but this effect is lost as sensitisation becomes established after 14 days.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results showing time-dependent changes in PrL-P function.

claim: TNTPrL-P.ChR2:hM4Di animals showed an aversion to the CNO paired chamber (post-conditioning–pre-conditioning time=−82.9±24.7 s, n=8).
source: TNTPrL-P.ChR2-hM4Di animals showed an aversion to the CNO paired chamber (post-conditioning–pre-conditioning time=−82.9±24.7 s, n=8; Figure 4B and C).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific quantitative data from behavioral experiments.

claim: TNTPrL-P.ChR2-hM4Di animals showed a significantly reduced preference score for the CNO paired chamber compared to the vehicle paired chamber (CNO paired vs vehicle paired=0.8±0.04 vs 1.06±0.06, p=0.04).
source: We calculated the preference of each rat for the CNO or vehicle paired chamber and found TNTPrL-P.ChR2-hM4Di animals showed a significantly reduced preference score compared to the vehicle paired chamber (Figure 4C; CNO paired vs vehicle paired=0.8±0.04 vs 1.06±0.06, paired t-test, p=0.04, n = 8).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific quantitative data with statistical analysis from behavioral experiments.

claim: TNTPrL-P.Control animals showed no difference in preference score for CNO and vehicle paired chambers (CNO paired vs vehicle paired=1.1±0.18 vs 1.00±0.21, p=0.81).
source: TNTPrL-P.Control animals showed no difference in preference score for CNO and vehicle paired chambers (Figure 4D, CNO paired vs vehicle paired=1.1±0.18 vs 1.00±0.21, paired t-test, p=0.81, n=9).
evidence: The manuscript describes control experiment results with statistical analysis.

claim: PrL-P neuronal activity opposes the development of negative affect in the immediate period after nerve injury.
source: These findings are consistent with PrL-P neuronal activity opposing the development of negative affect in the immediate period after nerve injury.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the place aversion experimental results.

claim: Opto-activation in TNTPrL-P.ChR2:hM4Di rats (20 Hz, 10 ms, 10–15 mW) produced an increase in the mechanical withdrawal threshold (baseline vs opto-activation vs recovery=1.7±0.5 vs 5.2±1.4 vs 2.1±0.5 g, p=0.02; baseline vs opto-activation, p=0.01).
source: Opto-activation in TNTPrL-P.ChR2:hM4Di rats (20 Hz, 10 ms, 10–15 mW) produced an increase in the mechanical withdrawal threshold (baseline vs opto-activation vs recovery=1.7±0.5 vs 5.2±1.4 vs 2.1±0.5 g, one-way repeated-measures (RM) ANOVA, p=0.02; Sidak's post-test baseline vs opto-activation, p=0.01, n=9; Figure 5B).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific quantitative data with statistical analysis from behavioral experiments.

claim: Equivalent illumination in TNTPrL-P.control rats did not change the mechanical withdrawal threshold (baseline vs opto-activation vs recovery=1.4±0.5 vs 1.0±0.4 vs 1.4±0.3, p=0.61).
source: Equivalent illumination in TNTPrL-P.control rats did not change the mechanical withdrawal threshold (baseline vs opto-activation vs recovery=1.4±0.5 vs 1.0±0.4 vs 1.4±0.3, one-way RM ANOVA, p=0.61, n=3; Figure 5B).
evidence: The manuscript describes control experiment results with statistical analysis.

claim: PrL-P neurons are still capable of supressing neuropathic sensitization in late-stage TNT rats.
source: This data indicates that the PrL-P neurons are still capable of supressing neuropathic sensitization in late-stage TNT rats.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the opto-activation experimental results in late-stage TNT rats.

claim: Opto-activation of PrL-P neurons reduced the number of action potentials evoked by a 4 g vF hair by 43% on average (baseline vs opto-activation vs recovery=25.7±5.0 vs 14.63±3.1 vs 25.0±45.0 action potentials; p=0.007; baseline vs opto-activation, p=0.009).
source: The number of action potentials evoked by a punctate mechanical stimulus with a 4 and 15 g vF hair was reduced on average by 43 and 23%, respectively (Figure 5D and E; 4 g vF, baseline vs opto-activation vs recovery=25.7±5.0 vs 14.63±3.1 vs 25.0±45.0 action potentials; mixed model [REML], fixed effect treatment, p=0.007; Dunnett's post-test baseline vs opto-activation, p=0.009, n=9; Figure 5E; 15 g vF, baseline vs opto-activation vs recovery=45.17±6.9 vs 34.5±6.9 vs 43.9±7.8; mixed model [REML], p=0.10, Dunnett's post-test baseline vs opto-activation, p=0.04, n=9).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific quantitative data with statistical analysis from electrophysiology experiments.

claim: Opto-activation of PrL-P neurons reduced the number of action potentials evoked by a 15 g vF hair by 23% on average (baseline vs opto-activation vs recovery=45.17±6.9 vs 34.5±6.9 vs 43.9±7.8; p=0.10, baseline vs opto-activation, p=0.04).
source: The number of action potentials evoked by a punctate mechanical stimulus with a 4 and 15 g vF hair was reduced on average by 43 and 23%, respectively (Figure 5D and E; 4 g vF, baseline vs opto-activation vs recovery=25.7±5.0 vs 14.63±3.1 vs 25.0±45.0 action potentials; mixed model [REML], fixed effect treatment, p=0.007; Dunnett's post-test baseline vs opto-activation, p=0.009, n=9; Figure 5E; 15 g vF, baseline vs opto-activation vs recovery=45.17±6.9 vs 34.5±6.9 vs 43.9±7.8; mixed model [REML], p=0.10, Dunnett's post-test baseline vs opto-activation, p=0.04, n=9).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific quantitative data with statistical analysis from electrophysiology experiments.

claim: Cold-evoked spinal WDR neuron activity was significantly reduced by opto-activation of PrL-P neurons by 47% on average (baseline vs opto-activation=172.0±38.8 vs 91.7±42.2 action potentials, p=0.04).
source: Similarly, cold-evoked spinal WDR neuron activity was significantly reduced by opto-activation of PrL-P neurons (Figure 5F, average reduction of 47%, baseline vs opto-activation=172.0±38.8 vs 91.7±42.2 action potentials, paired t-test, p=0.04, n=4).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific quantitative data with statistical analysis from electrophysiology experiments.

claim: PrL-P neurons are acting to suppress neuropathic sensitisation (punctate and cold allodynia) at a spinal level through the engagement of the DPMS.
source: This data indicates that the PrL-P neurons are acting to suppress neuropathic sensitisation (punctate and cold allodynia) at a spinal level through the engagement of the DPMS.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the electrophysiology experimental results.

claim: In uninjured animals, PrL-P neurons exert tonic inhibitory control over evoked noxious withdrawal responses.
source: In uninjured animals, we found PrL-P neurons to exert tonic inhibitory control over evoked noxious withdrawal responses, suggesting they were involved with the moment-to-moment regulation of nocifensive behaviour.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the experimental results in naive animals.

claim: Following tibial nerve injury, rats developed mechanical and thermal allodynia that plateaued at around 14 days post injury.
source: Following tibial nerve injury, rats developed mechanical and thermal allodynia that plateaued at around 14 days post injury.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental observations from the TNT model.

claim: There is a tonic activity in PrL-P neurons that suppresses hypersensitivity early after nerve ligation, but this is lost with time as the neuropathic pain phenotype emerges.
source: These findings are consistent with there being a tonic activity in PrL-P neurons that suppresses hypersensitivity early after nerve ligation, but this is lost with time as the neuropathic pain phenotype emerges.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the longitudinal experimental results.

claim: Despite the loss in function, opto-activation of PrL-P neurons during later stages of neuropathic pain produces anti-allodynic effects in neuropathic animals achieved, at least in part, by inhibitory effects on spinal nociceptive processing.
source: Despite the loss in function, opto-activation of PrL-P neurons during later stages of neuropathic pain produces anti-allodynic effects in neuropathic animals achieved, at least in part, by inhibitory effects on spinal nociceptive processing.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the opto-activation and electrophysiology experimental results.

claim: It is the loss of cortical drive to the DPMS which is a major contributor to the expression of neuropathic sensitisation after nerve injury.
source: We postulate that this cortical–midbrain–spinal network allows executive control of nociception and regulation of pain, and that it is the loss of cortical drive to the DPMS, which is a major contributor to the expression of neuropathic sensitisation after nerve injury.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the overall experimental findings.

claim: Loss of endogenous inhibitory control of CNS pain processing is a shared feature of a wide variety of human chronic pain conditions.
source: Loss of endogenous inhibitory control of CNS pain processing (Staud, 2012) and altered functional connectivity between the mPFC and the PAG is a shared feature of a wide variety of human chronic pain conditions (Jensen et al., 2012; Yu et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2017; Segerdahl et al., 2018)—our findings suggest these changes are causally related.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Altered functional connectivity between the mPFC and the PAG is a shared feature of a wide variety of human chronic pain conditions.
source: Loss of endogenous inhibitory control of CNS pain processing (Staud, 2012) and altered functional connectivity between the mPFC and the PAG is a shared feature of a wide variety of human chronic pain conditions (Jensen et al., 2012; Yu et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2017; Segerdahl et al., 2018)—our findings suggest these changes are causally related.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The findings suggest that loss of endogenous inhibitory control and altered functional connectivity between the mPFC and PAG are causally related.
source: Loss of endogenous inhibitory control of CNS pain processing (Staud, 2012) and altered functional connectivity between the mPFC and the PAG is a shared feature of a wide variety of human chronic pain conditions (Jensen et al., 2012; Yu et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2017; Segerdahl et al., 2018)—our findings suggest these changes are causally related.
evidence: This is an interpretation connecting the current findings to previous literature.

claim: The human mPFC, including the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), is increasingly recognised as a key locus in the development and maintenance of chronic pain.
source: The human mPFC, including the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), is increasingly recognised as a key locus in the development and maintenance of chronic pain, with changes in structure and function that are associated with, and sometimes predictive of, the transition to chronic pain (Apkarian et al., 2004; Baliki et al., 2012; Hashmi et al., 2013; Baliki and Apkarian, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Changes in structure and function of the mPFC are associated with, and sometimes predictive of, the transition to chronic pain.
source: The human mPFC, including the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), is increasingly recognised as a key locus in the development and maintenance of chronic pain, with changes in structure and function that are associated with, and sometimes predictive of, the transition to chronic pain (Apkarian et al., 2004; Baliki et al., 2012; Hashmi et al., 2013; Baliki and Apkarian, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The PAG is a key node in the DPMS.
source: The PAG is not only a key node in the DPMS but also an important orchestrator of autonomic and sensorimotor systems that is engaged to support mPFC function in aversive learning, emotional modulation, and pain modulation, which are all relevant to the chronic pain phenotype (Keay and Bandler, 2001; Franklin et al., 2017; Rozeske et al., 2018; Huang et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The PAG is an important orchestrator of autonomic and sensorimotor systems that is engaged to support mPFC function in aversive learning, emotional modulation, and pain modulation.
source: The PAG is not only a key node in the DPMS but also an important orchestrator of autonomic and sensorimotor systems that is engaged to support mPFC function in aversive learning, emotional modulation, and pain modulation, which are all relevant to the chronic pain phenotype (Keay and Bandler, 2001; Franklin et al., 2017; Rozeske et al., 2018; Huang et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In humans, changes in functional connectivity between the mPFC/ACC and PAG are commonly observed in experimental paradigms that produce emotional, attentional, and placebo/nocebo influences on pain.
source: In humans, changes in functional connectivity between the mPFC/ACC and PAG are commonly observed in experimental paradigms that produce emotional, attentional, and placebo/nocebo influences on pain as well following the delivery of analgesic drugs and often interpreted as reflecting engagement of the DPMS (Wager et al., 2004; Wiech et al., 2014; Wanigasekera et al., 2018; Oliva et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Changes in functional connectivity between the mPFC/ACC and PAG are often interpreted as reflecting engagement of the DPMS.
source: In humans, changes in functional connectivity between the mPFC/ACC and PAG are commonly observed in experimental paradigms that produce emotional, attentional, and placebo/nocebo influences on pain as well following the delivery of analgesic drugs and often interpreted as reflecting engagement of the DPMS (Wager et al., 2004; Wiech et al., 2014; Wanigasekera et al., 2018; Oliva et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Changes in the functional connectivity between regions of the mPFC and the PAG are often correlated with changes in pain perception and/or disease progression.
source: Moreover, changes in the functional connectivity between regions of the mPFC and the PAG are often correlated with changes in pain perception and/or disease progression (Cifre et al., 2012; Hemington and Coulombe, 2015; Harper et al., 2018; Segerdahl et al., 2018; Wanigasekera et al., 2018; González-Roldán et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The PrL, a component of the rodent mPFC, can engage the DPMS to affect nociception.
source: Here, we provide evidence in rodents that the PrL, a component of the rodent mPFC, can engage the DPMS to affect nociception, and loss in PrL-P neuron function is causally related to the development of the neuropathic pain state in rats.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings from the current study.

claim: Loss in PrL-P neuron function is causally related to the development of the neuropathic pain state in rats.
source: Here, we provide evidence in rodents that the PrL, a component of the rodent mPFC, can engage the DPMS to affect nociception, and loss in PrL-P neuron function is causally related to the development of the neuropathic pain state in rats.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the experimental findings from the current study.

claim: Changes in functional communication between the mPFC and PAG, whether trait-, age- or disease-related, likely manifest as alterations in the descending control of spinal nociception.
source: We suggest that changes in functional communication between the mPFC and PAG, whether trait-, age- or disease-related, likely manifest as alterations in the descending control of spinal nociception.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation extending the current findings to broader contexts.

claim: In neuropathic rodents, at 7–10 days post-nerve injury, there is a decline in spontaneous and evoked PrL layer five pyramidal cell activity including those that project to the PAG.
source: In neuropathic rodents, at 7–10 days post-nerve injury, there is a decline in spontaneous and evoked PrL layer five pyramidal cell activity including those that project to the PAG (Cheriyan and Sheets, 2018; Mitrić et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The reduction in PrL projection neurons excitability is produced in part by enhanced feedforward inhibition from local GABAergic interneurons and driven by inputs from the basolateral amygdala.
source: This reduction in PrL projection neurons excitability is produced in part by enhanced feedforward inhibition from local GABAergic interneurons and driven by inputs from the basolateral amygdala (Zhang et al., 2015; Cheriyan et al., 2016; Kiritoshi et al., 2016; Cheriyan and Sheets, 2018; Huang et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Opto-inhibition of BLA inputs to the PrL releases PrL-P neurons to engage descending inhibitory control from the PAG.
source: Opto-inhibition of BLA inputs to the PrL releases PrL-P neurons to engage descending inhibitory control from the PAG (Huang et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: PrL-P neurons are glutamatergic and target both GABAergic and glutamatergic neurons in the PAG.
source: PrL-P neurons are glutamatergic and target both GABAergic and glutamatergic neurons in the PAG (Franklin et al., 2017; Huang et al., 2019) but engage descending inhibitory control from the PAG that is associated with the release of local GABAergic control (Tovote et al., 2016; Huang et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: PrL-P neurons engage descending inhibitory control from the PAG that is associated with the release of local GABAergic control.
source: PrL-P neurons are glutamatergic and target both GABAergic and glutamatergic neurons in the PAG (Franklin et al., 2017; Huang et al., 2019) but engage descending inhibitory control from the PAG that is associated with the release of local GABAergic control (Tovote et al., 2016; Huang et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The BLA–PrL–PAG–spinal network is central to the expression of neuropathic pain.
source: We suggest that the BLA–PrL–PAG–spinal network is central to the expression of neuropathic pain and therapeutics that reengage cortical control of descending pain modulation may be effective in treating both sensory and affective disturbances in chronic pain.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the current and previous findings.

claim: Therapeutics that reengage cortical control of descending pain modulation may be effective in treating both sensory and affective disturbances in chronic pain.
source: We suggest that the BLA–PrL–PAG–spinal network is central to the expression of neuropathic pain and therapeutics that reengage cortical control of descending pain modulation may be effective in treating both sensory and affective disturbances in chronic pain.
evidence: This is a speculative suggestion for therapeutic approaches based on the findings.

claim: While BLA inputs to the PrL drive sensory hypersensitivity and negative affect by reducing descending inhibition of the spinal dorsal horn, BLA inputs to the dorsal cingulate regions mitigate pain-related aversion.
source: However, while BLA inputs to the PrL drive sensory hypersensitivity and negative affect by reducing descending inhibition of the spinal dorsal horn, BLA inputs to the dorsal cingulate regions mitigate pain-related aversion (Meda et al., 2019).

claim: In neuropathic animals, peripherally evoked spinal dorsal horn WDR neurons are inhibited by PrL-P neuronal activity.

claim: Spinal WDR neurons are a known target of descending modulatory systems.

claim: The PrL is able to affect nociceptive information early in the ascending pathway, likely prior to extensive integration with other nociceptive/non-nociceptive information.
source: It is significant from a therapeutic perspective that the PrL is able to affect nociceptive information early in the ascending pathway, likely prior to extensive integration with other nociceptive/non-nociceptive information, which would allow for selective and potent actions on the pain experience and pain state development (Heinricher et al., 2009).

claim: Antagonism of spinal alpha2-adrenoceptors reveals contralateral allodynia.

claim: Potentiation of spinal NA signalling with reuptake inhibitors can prevent the development of neuropathic pain and reverse neuropathic hypersensitivity in late-stage neuropathic animals.
